why: The PATHS in this file are re-derived every run and are here only so a drift has something to disagree with. The READING is not re-derivable: what a file DOES with the stamp it matched is a human reading, so it is a datum and never a guess. An unread file is `reads: null` and the gate SHORTFALLs on its own debt rather than passing over it.

`anchored` applies to a `time` reading alone. True means the instant comes from a stamp owner that bounds the digit run, with the components range-validated in the owner or at its call site (`DexClock.fileStamp`, a local `_mkTMs` / `stampMk`, `writers.file_start_stamp` plus the caller's `strptime`, `nightqc.floating_stamp_s`). False means the file slices the digits into a bare `Date.UTC` or `strptime` itself. Every other reading computes no instant, so §∅ makes its `anchored` null.

🔴 THE POPULATION ERASED THE REPAIR IT CERTIFIED. A reader is repaired by handing the whole basename to a stamp owner and ceasing to slice digits, which is exactly when it stops spelling a 14-digit run — so membership LEFT on the commit that fixed the file, the departure check saw a file that had never been declared, and the headline counted the files that still spell a stamp rather than the files that read one. `STAMP_OWNERS` is the second predicate: a declared owner vocabulary, read over comment-blanked source, with a definition excluded because an owner does not consume itself. Eight files entered on it, every one a time reader, and membership is now monotone under the repair.

AND THE READING WAS KEYED ON THE SPELLING SITE. Five declarations above carry `READ AGAIN 2026-10-27`: each described what the file's 14-digit regex does while its code called an owner elsewhere and did something else with the answer. `oxydex-dsp.js` read `docstring` and converts a filename stamp to an instant at two sites. A reading is a property of the FILE, so it is now read against every site the file has, not against the one the predicate matched.
readBy is per entry where it is not the file-level reader: Heron read the 28 files of the first census, Magpie read the eight that entered on the owner predicate and re-read the five marked above.

The parent census's predicate was the literal source text `\d{14}`, so it saw one spelling of one read. Twelve files here spell the same fourteen digits out and were invisible to it — among them two the parent credited as FIXED, because a file with two readers leaves a spelling-keyed census when one reader is repaired.

Its predicate admits a file by the spelling and computes no instant, which is exactly an accept test. Its own sum-to-14 runs are the header prose, the selftest fixtures and the atom pattern itself. Excluding it would be the one hole a census cannot afford: the file that decides membership would be the only one nobody re-derives. It entered the population the moment git tracked it, which is also the measurement that found this. READ AGAIN 2026-10-27 (Magpie): it is now admitted by BOTH predicates, and the second one is its own test data — the selftest fixtures for the owner predicate write `DexClock.fileStamp(` and `stampMk(` as literal strings, and the census reads a string exactly as it reads a call, having no parser by design. Its owner sites are therefore fixtures, not stamp reads, and the reading stays accept-test.

cpapdex-dsp.js.note: THE ONE TIME READER THAT SLICES THE DIGITS ITSELF, and the separator rule is why nobody had seen it. Its node-local `parseTimestamp` holds the Clock Contract's 14-digit arm at line 85 and spells the gap `[_\-]?`, so the run ended there and the file reached neither predicate until 2026-10-27. CPAPDex carries no `clock.js` by design, so there is no owner to route to and the node-local variant is correct to exist. `anchored` is false because the regex bounds no run: it range-validates through `_ckMk` and then takes the first fourteen digits of a longer token. Logged as its own row rather than repaired here, because the fix re-bundles CPAPDex.
